title: The Sharpe Pint: Bad News, Big Bets, and the Seed Lottery

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent your weekend trying to figure out how a US jobs report that missed by a mile somehow sent the S&P 500 to a fresh record high, welcome to the club. It is the classic 'bad news is good news' macro circus, and we are all just trying to keep our pints steady while the Fed juggles. Today, we are diving into the mega-LBO of Electronic Arts, Mastercard's big-money stablecoin bet, and why your colleague's reinforcement learning backtest is almost certainly a statistical fairy tale. Grab a coffee—or something stronger—and let's get into it.

content.text: Bad News is Good News: US Jobs Shock Sparks Record Stock Rally

The US economy threw a proper spanner in the works on Friday, unexpectedly shedding 23,000 jobs in July when economists were bracing for a comfortable 80,000 gain. To make matters worse, the Labor Department quietly shaved another 103,000 jobs off May and June's figures. While the headline unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, it was for all the wrong reasons—namely, people giving up and dropping out of the active workforce entirely.

Why it matters: In the upside-down world of macro trading, bad news is the ultimate fuel. The sudden chill in the labour market has effectively killed off any lingering fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes this year. Bond yields tumbled, with the 10-year Treasury yield sliding to 4.64%, while equity markets went on an absolute tear. The S&P 500 rose 0.6% to a record 7,757.64, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped 1.3% to 26,690.62, capping off the best weekly rally for major US indexes since mid-April.

The City Angle: For asset managers and macro desks, this is the classic 'bad news is good news' trade. However, the clock is ticking. If payrolls continue to contract, the market's narrative will shift rapidly from a celebratory 'rates are staying on hold' to a panicked 'are we staring down the barrel of a hard landing?'

What to say at the pub: 'It's a textbook macro pivot. The Fed is officially done, but if we get another negative payroll print next month, the equity bulls are going to start looking very exposed. Keep an eye on defensive sectors.'
Game Over for Public Markets: EA's Record-Breaking $55bn Take-Private Closes

The mega-LBO is officially back, and it’s wearing a gaming headset. The colossal $55 billion take-private of Electronic Arts (EA)—the powerhouse behind FIFA/EA Sports FC, Battlefield, and The Sims—has officially closed. The deal, backed by a heavyweight consortium of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), Silver Lake, and Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners, is the largest all-cash sponsor take-private in history. EA has now been delisted from the Nasdaq.

Why it matters: This isn't just a massive corporate reshuffle; it’s a structural shift in how global entertainment is funded. The deal is loaded with a whopping $20 billion in debt, and PIF now holds the majority stake. It underscores a broader trend of sovereign wealth funds moving from passive, minority stake-building to outright, hands-on control of major cultural and intellectual property.

The City Angle: For investment bankers and private equity analysts, this is a masterclass in mega-scale leverage. Squeezing a $55bn company into a private structure in this rate environment requires serious cojones—and the bottomless pockets of Gulf sovereign wealth to anchor the equity. The focus now shifts to how they manage that massive debt load, with rumours of $700 million in annual cost cuts already circulating.

What to say in an interview: 'The EA deal shows that sovereign wealth funds are transitioning from passive capital allocators to active operators. Taking a massive IP engine private allows them to escape the tyranny of quarterly earnings and invest in long-term gaming franchises, but carrying $20bn in debt means we’re likely to see aggressive monetisation and cost-cutting in the near term.'
Mastercard's Stablecoin Bet: A $1.8bn Bridge to the On-Chain Economy

Mastercard has completed its acquisition of London-based stablecoin infrastructure provider BVNK for up to $1.8 billion ($1.5bn upfront, plus $300m in performance-based earnouts). It is a massive statement of intent from the payments giant, which is actively building the plumbing to connect traditional fiat currency rails with on-chain stablecoin and tokenised deposit networks.

Why it matters: Stablecoins are no longer just a playground for crypto traders; they are rapidly scaling into the real economy. In 2025, digital currency payment volumes topped $350 billion, driven by real-world demand for cross-border B2B payments, remittances, and corporate treasury flows. Mastercard’s acquisition of BVNK is a direct bet on a 'multi-money' future where fiat and digital currencies coexist seamlessly.

The City Angle: For fintech analysts and transaction bankers, this is a clear defensive play. Traditional card networks face a structural threat from cheap, instant, blockchain-based settlement. By buying the leading infrastructure provider, Mastercard is ensuring it owns the tolls on the new digital highways rather than letting upstart crypto networks bypass them entirely.

What to say at work: 'Mastercard isn't waiting around for central banks to launch CBDCs. By acquiring BVNK, they are integrating stablecoin rails directly into their global network. It’s a massive validation of stablecoins as a superior technology for cross-border B2B payments, where SWIFT is still too slow and expensive.'
The Coldcard Exploit: A $100m Crack in Crypto's Safest Vaults

The ultimate myth of crypto self-custody has been shattered. A catastrophic firmware flaw in Coldcard hardware wallets (made by Toronto-based Coinkite) allowed hackers to reverse-engineer and guess wallet seed phrases due to weak entropy generation. Over 1,755 Bitcoin (worth roughly $110 million) have been drained from thousands of 'offline' wallets, leaving some of the most security-conscious investors in the space completely wiped out.

Why it matters: Cold wallets are supposed to be the gold standard of security because they are entirely disconnected from the internet. This exploit proves that offline storage is an illusion if the underlying math generating the keys is broken. The irony is thick: Coinkite moved its code from open-source to a restrictive 'source-verifiable' license in 2021, which critics argue prevented independent developers from spotting and fixing the bug years ago.

The City Angle: The hack has triggered a massive, unexpected flight to safety—not out of Bitcoin, but into institutional custody. US spot Bitcoin ETFs had their best week since April, pulling in $853.5 million in the week ending August 7. Wealthy investors and family offices are realising that managing their own keys is a massive operational risk, and they’d rather pay BlackRock or Fidelity a few basis points to handle the custody.

What to say at the pub: 'The Coldcard hack is a brutal reminder of the operational risks of self-custody. It completely reframes the institutional crypto thesis. Custody isn't just a storage problem; it's a governance and insurance problem. This is a massive structural tailwind for Coinbase Custody and the spot ETFs.'
Nuclear Medicine Gets Hot: Curium and Lantheus Merge in $8bn Deal

The radiopharmaceutical land grab is accelerating. Curium, a global leader in nuclear medicine controlled by private equity firm CapVest Partners, has agreed to acquire Nasdaq-listed rival Lantheus Holdings in a deal valued at up to $8 billion. Lantheus shareholders will receive $102.50 per share in cash at closing, plus up to $12 per share in Contingent Value Rights (CVRs) tied to commercial milestones through 2030.

Why it matters: Radiopharmaceuticals—which use targeted radiation to diagnose and treat cancer, a field known as 'theranostics'—are the hottest sector in healthcare M&A. The supply chain is notoriously brutal because these medical isotopes have half-lives measured in hours, meaning they cannot be warehoused. This merger unites Curium's massive global manufacturing network with Lantheus's dominant US diagnostic portfolio, including its blockbuster prostate cancer imaging agent, Pylarify.

The City Angle: For healthcare investment bankers and private equity professionals, this is a textbook roll-up. CapVest is building an integrated, end-to-end global giant capable of fending off mega-cap pharma players like Novartis and AstraZeneca, who have been aggressively buying up radiopharma assets. The use of CVRs is also a clever way to bridge valuation gaps in a volatile market.

What to say in an interview: 'The Curium-Lantheus merger is all about securing the supply chain. In radiopharma, manufacturing and distribution are the ultimate moats because of isotope decay. By combining Curium's global production sites with Lantheus's US diagnostic footprint, they are creating an unbeatable end-to-end platform that will be highly attractive to a mega-pharma buyer down the road.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The "Bad News is Good News" Party

Friday’s session was a classic exhibition of the market’s favourite twisted logic: bad economic news is a glorious excuse to buy the dip. The S&P 500 climbed 0.62% to close at a fresh record high of 7,757.64, capping off a stellar 3.58% gain for the week. The tech-heavy Nasdaq led the charge, jumping 1.3% on Friday to 26,690.62 (up 5.2% on the week), while the small-cap Russell 2000 added 1.1% to close at 3,034.49. The catalyst? A US nonfarm payrolls report that didn't just miss expectations—it fell down the stairs, dropped its pint, and took the consensus forecast with it. The US economy unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, while May and June figures were revised down by a combined 103,000.
The Fed's Tight-Lipped Chair Gets a Reality Check

To understand why a shrinking job market has traders popping champagne, you have to look at what the Federal Reserve has been up to. Under new Chair Kevin Warsh, who took the helm in May, the Fed has been playing a very hawkish, very quiet game. Warsh has famously tried to untether the bond market from Fed forward guidance, dodging questions and leaving the door wide open for a rate hike at the September meeting after a highly divided 9-3 vote in July. Markets had been pricing in a September hike to combat sticky energy inflation. The -23,000 jobs print was a massive bucket of ice water over the Fed's hawkish bonfire. Treasury yields tumbled, with the 10-year yield falling to 4.64% and the 2-year dropping to 4.20%, as traders rapidly priced out the likelihood of near-term tightening.
Gold Goes Parabolic as Hormuz Tensions Boil

While equities celebrated a gentler Fed, the real fireworks were in the commodities complex. Gold surged a massive 2.41% on Friday to close at $4,353.23 per ounce, wrapping up its best week since January with a whopping 7%+ gain. Silver followed suit, jumping 2.78% to $64.31. While the weaker dollar and falling yields provided the macro fuel, the structural bid is pure geopolitics. Over the weekend, Iran issued a list of maximalist demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz—which has been blockaded since late February—demanding the US lift its naval blockade, withdraw forces, and pay "complete compensation" for war damages. To drive the point home, an Emirati ADNOC tanker was targeted by an Iranian missile on Saturday. With LNG exports through the strait down 95%, the geopolitical risk premium is keeping a massive floor under both gold and Brent crude, which rose 1.3% to $83.55.
The 47% Earnings Growth Illusion

If you’ve been looking at the Q2 earnings season headlines, you’d be forgiven for thinking corporate America is in the middle of an unprecedented golden age. Blended earnings growth for the S&P 500 is currently sitting at a jaw-dropping 47.4%, with companies beating estimates by an aggregate 29.2%—the largest positive surprise since FactSet began tracking the metric in 2008. But before you put your house on the index, let's look at the plumbing. This "record-breaking" season comes with a massive, multi-billion-dollar asterisk:

items: Alphabet's paper profit: Google's parent company reported a GAAP EPS that included a massive $98 billion non-operating gain, primarily driven by unrealised gains on its equity securities portfolio.
Amazon's Anthropic bump: Amazon’s earnings were similarly inflated by a $53.4 billion paper gain from its investment in AI startup Anthropic.
The real picture: If you strip out these two non-operating paper gains, the aggregate S&P 500 earnings surprise plummets from 29.2% to a much more terrestrial (though still respectable) 10.9%.

content.text: It’s a classic reminder of why you never buy the headline without checking the cash flow statement. Stripping out paper gains reveals a corporate landscape that is healthy, but far from the blowout the media is reporting.
The Cross-Asset Read: Stretched to the Limit?

So, where does this leave us? On one hand, the "bad news is good news" trade is back in full swing. On the other, Bank of America’s Bull & Bear Indicator has just climbed to 9.7—its highest level since 2021. In the world of sentiment indicators, that is deep in "extreme bullishness" territory, which is historically a highly reliable contrarian sell signal. The market is currently priced for a flawless soft landing where inflation politely vanishes, the Fed stops hiking, and we all live happily ever after. But if the labour market is genuinely cracking, those paper-thin earnings multiples are going to look very exposed.

content.text: The Twin Devils of Mortgage-Backed Securities: Contraction and Extension Risk

If you have ever looked at the yield on an Agency Mortgage-Backed Security (MBS) and thought, "Blimey, that is a decent spread over Treasuries with basically zero credit risk," you have stumbled into one of the classic traps of fixed income. That extra yield is not a free lunch. It is the premium you are paid for selling a highly valuable, free option to millions of suburban homeowners. That option is the right to prepay their mortgage at any time, and it exposes you to the twin devils of MBS investing: contraction risk and extension risk.
The Concept: Negative Convexity

When you buy a standard corporate bond, you know exactly when you will get your principal back (barring a default). But an MBS is a pool of residential mortgages. Homeowners do not behave like corporate treasurers; they behave like normal people. If interest rates fall, they refinance to save money. If interest rates rise, they stay put. This means as an MBS investor, you are short a call option. This option creates negative convexity, which is a fancy way of saying: "Heads they win, tails you lose."

items: Contraction Risk (Rates Fall): When interest rates drop, homeowners rush to refinance their mortgages. The principal is paid back to you much faster than expected. Your bond's Weighted Average Life (WAL) contracts. You get your cash back early, but now you have to reinvest it in a market where yields are miserably low.

Extension Risk (Rates Rise): When interest rates spike, homeowners cling to their cheap, locked-in mortgages like gold. Nobody refinances, and nobody moves house. The principal repayments dry up, and your bond's WAL extends. Your money is now trapped in a low-yielding asset for years longer than you planned, right when you could be reinvesting at higher market rates.

content.text: A Simple Example with Numbers
Let us say you buy an Agency MBS at par with an expected Weighted Average Life (WAL) of 5 years, yielding 6%.

items: Scenario A (Rates drop to 3%): Homeowners refinance en masse. Your 5-year WAL suddenly shrinks to 1.5 years. You get your principal back rapidly, but you can only reinvest it at the new 3% rate. This is contraction risk.

Scenario B (Rates jump to 8%): Refinancing stops entirely. Your 5-year WAL stretches out to 12 years. You are stuck holding a 6% yielding asset for over a decade while the rest of the market is paying 8%. This is extension risk.

content.text: Why It Matters in Asset Management and Markets

Because MBS durations are constantly shifting with interest rates, portfolio managers cannot just buy them and forget them. They have to engage in dynamic hedging (or convexity hedging). If rates rise, the duration of their MBS portfolio extends, making the portfolio more sensitive to further rate hikes. To offset this, managers must sell long-term Treasuries or pay fixed on interest rate swaps to bring their duration back in line. In volatile markets, this can trigger a feedback loop—rising rates force MBS managers to sell Treasuries, which pushes rates even higher. This is exactly what caused the infamous "Great Bond Massacre" of 1994.
Common Beginner Mistake

The most common mistake is using Modified Duration to analyse MBS. Modified duration assumes that cash flows are static and do not change when interest rates move. For MBS, this is a financial sin. You must use Effective Duration, which uses pricing models (like Monte Carlo simulations based on historical prepayment speeds) to estimate how the cash flows themselves will shift as interest rates change.
How to Ace This in an Interview
If an interviewer asks you to explain MBS prepayment risk or negative convexity, do not just recite a textbook definition. Walk them through the homeowner's incentive structure.

"An MBS investor is essentially short a call option written to the homeowner. When rates fall, the homeowner exercises that option to refinance, forcing the investor to reinvest at lower rates (contraction risk). When rates rise, the homeowner holds onto their cheap rate, locking the investor’s capital in a low-yielding asset (extension risk). This asymmetry is negative convexity, which is why MBS trade at a spread over Treasuries—to compensate investors for this cash-flow volatility."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Seed Lottery: Why Your Mate's RL Backtest is a Lie

We’ve all been there. A colleague walks over, smugly showing off a new Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) trading model with a Sharpe of 2.0 and a CAGR that could buy a small island. You look at the code, and it seems fine. But here is the dirty little secret of financial RL: it is incredibly sensitive to the random seed. Run the exact same model with a different seed (which changes the initial neural network weights or the order of training batches), and that beautiful Sharpe of 2.0 might collapse into a miserable 0.8. In the quant world, this leads to 'seed-picking'—running ten seeds and only showing the boss the lucky one.
The Idea: Intent-to-Treat Reporting

To stop this statistical cherry-picking, a brilliant paper by Marwan Elgoghel (Monmouth University) titled 'Every Seed, Every Result: Intent-to-Treat Reporting for Financial Reinforcement Learning' borrows a concept from clinical medical trials: Intent-to-Treat (ITT). In medicine, ITT means you must analyse every patient randomised into the trial, even if they dropped out or refused their pills. In quant finance, ITT reporting means you must pre-register your random seeds, prohibit post-hoc exclusions, and publish the complete run ledger of every single seed.
The Damage of Seed-Picking

How much does seed-picking actually inflate performance? Elgoghel tested a Deep RL model on a US large-cap portfolio. By simply running five seeds and reporting the best one, the performance metrics were massively inflated compared to the median of all runs:

items: Sharpe Ratio: Inflated by 15% (reaching 1.99 instead of the median 1.73).
CAGR: Inflated by a whopping 94% (71.4% vs the median 36.8%).
Information Ratio: Inflated by 137%.

content.text: This is enough to turn a completely average, unviable strategy into a headline-grabbing 'holy grail' backtest, without changing a single line of the underlying algorithm. It’s pure, unadulterated seed luck.
A Mini Technical Example

To implement an ITT workflow, you should pre-register a set of seeds, run them all, and report the entire distribution (or at least the median and variance), rather than just returning the best-performing model. Here is how you might structure a simple evaluation loop in Python:

import numpy as np
from my_rl_library import TradingEnv, DRLAgent

# 1. Pre-register your seeds (no changing them later!)
PRE_REGISTERED_SEEDS = [42, 137, 2026, 888, 999]
run_ledger = []

for seed in PRE_REGISTERED_SEEDS:
    # Set all random states for reproducibility
    np.random.seed(seed)
    env = TradingEnv(seed=seed)
    agent = DRLAgent(seed=seed)
    
    # Train and evaluate on held-out test data
    agent.train(env)
    test_metrics = agent.evaluate_on_test_set()
    
    run_ledger.append({
        "seed": seed,
        "sharpe": test_metrics["sharpe"],
        "cagr": test_metrics["cagr"]
    })

# 2. Report the full ledger, not just the max!
sharpes = [run["sharpe"] for run in run_ledger]
print(f"Best Seed Sharpe (The Lie): {max(sharpes):.2f}")
print(f"Median Seed Sharpe (The Truth): {np.median(sharpes):.2f}")
print(f"Seed Variance: {np.var(sharpes):.4f}")
How to Use This in the Pub or an Interview
Next time a quant candidate or a colleague presents a reinforcement learning model with stellar backtest results, drop this question:
"How sensitive is this strategy to the random seed? Did you pre-register your seeds and run an intent-to-treat analysis, or are we looking at the survivor of a seed lottery?"

It’s a killer question. It immediately shows you understand that RL is notoriously high-variance and that 'phantom alpha' is often just a lucky weight initialisation. If they look like a deer in headlights, you know they’ve cherry-picked.
The Catch

The obvious limitation is computational cost. If your deep RL model takes three days to train on an expensive GPU cluster, running 10 pre-registered seeds means 30 days of compute. But as the paper argues, if you can’t afford to run multiple seeds, you can’t afford to trust the results. A single-seed backtest in RL is essentially a lottery ticket.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Five Sins of Financial LLMs

If you have spent any time in a City meeting room over the last year, you have likely endured a pitch from a vendor (or an over-enthusiastic internal quant) claiming their new LLM-based trading agent has a Sharpe ratio that would make Jim Simons blush. But before you hand over the keys to the firm's capital, there is a paper you absolutely must read. Published in early 2026 and presented at ICML, 'Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration' is a brilliant, cold-shower of a position paper that exposes why almost all academic and commercial benchmarks for financial AI are, to put it politely, complete bollocks.
Why This Paper?

The paper is co-authored by a heavy-hitting team from the University of Oxford, Chicago Booth, BlackRock, and the University of Florida (including Alejandro Lopez-Lira, who famously proved ChatGPT could predict stock moves back in 2023). They reviewed 164 papers on financial LLMs published between 2023 and 2025. Their verdict? The vast majority of reported 'alpha' is just a mirage created by basic backtesting sins that any first-year analyst should be fired for committing. In fact, they found that not a single one of the five major financial biases was discussed in more than 28% of the studies.
The Five Sins of Financial LLM Evaluation

items: Look-Ahead Bias (The Time-Traveller): Only 26.8% of studies acknowledged this. This happens when the LLM's pre-training data or RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieval window includes information from the 'future' relative to the trade date. If an LLM is trained on data up to 2025, asking it to 'predict' 2024 stock returns is just a test of its memory, not its trading acumen.

Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Buster): Acknowledged by a microscopic 1.2% of papers. Most evaluations test LLMs on a static universe of current S&P 500 or FTSE 100 companies. This completely ignores the companies that went bust or got delisted during the backtest period. It is easy to look like a genius when you only pick from survivors.

Narrative Bias (The Bullshitter): LLMs are designed to be fluent and persuasive. They excel at spinning a beautifully coherent story about why a stock went up, even if the reasoning is entirely hallucinated or completely disconnected from the actual causal drivers. It creates an 'illusion of understanding' that masks underlying complexity.

Objective Bias (The Confident Guesser): Standard LLM training rewards the model for completing a prompt, which forces it to guess confidently even when it has no idea. In finance, knowing when not to trade is often more valuable than trading. Forcing a model to guess converts ignorance into false precision.

Cost Bias (The Paper-Trading Dreamer): Many papers report spectacular returns while completely ignoring transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, market impact, and inference latency. A strategy that requires making 100 trades a day based on real-time LLM API calls will quickly see its alpha eaten alive by trading fees and API latency.

content.text: "These biases break financial tasks in distinct ways and they often compound to create an illusion of validity... structural validity should be enforced before any result is used to support a deployment claim."
The Fix: The Structural Validity Framework

Instead of just throwing stones, the authors propose a practical 'Structural Validity Framework'—a checklist designed to act as a flight simulator for financial AI before it hits real-world markets. It has five core pillars:

items: Temporal Sanitation: Enforcing strict 'non-anticipativity'. This means verifying knowledge cutoffs and ensuring RAG systems only retrieve documents that were actually public at time t.
Dynamic Universe Construction: Dynamically updating the asset universe at each step of the backtest to include delisted and bankrupt firms.

Epistemic Calibration: Designing the model's action space to include 'No Trade' or 'I don't know' as legitimate, high-scoring options. The model must output calibrated confidence scores that risk controllers can actually use.

Rationale Robustness: Treating explanations as testable hypotheses (e.g., using entity substitution tests to see if the LLM's logic holds when company names are swapped) rather than just decorative text.
Realistic Implementation Constraints: Deducting transaction costs, slippage, and LLM generation latency from the final performance metrics.

content.text: What to Skim and What to Read

If you are short on time, skip the heavy mathematical formulations of temporal sanitation in Section 2. Instead, focus on Section 3, which breaks down the 'Five Sins' with concrete examples of how they manifest in financial tasks, and Section 4, which outlines the checklist. The authors have also released an open-source web tool and automatic bias detector on GitHub (Eleanorkong/Awesome-Financial-LLM-Bias-Mitigation) which is well worth bookmarking.
How This Connects to You

Whether you are a quant building these systems, an asset manager evaluating third-party tools, or an investment banker preparing for an interview, this paper is your shield. The next time a vendor or colleague shows you a backtest of an LLM-based strategy, you now have the exact toolkit to dismantle it. It shifts the conversation from 'look how smart this AI is' to 'how did you control for look-ahead bias in your RAG pipeline?'
What to Say Over a Pint

Most of the academic papers claiming LLMs can beat the market are just high-tech memory tests. They are evaluating models on data they have already seen during pre-training, or testing them on a survivor-biased stock list while ignoring transaction costs. If your AI trading agent cannot say 'I don't know' and does not factor in API latency, it is not an investment strategy—it is just an expensive hallucination engine.

content.text: The Myth of the 'Mental Itch' (And the Real Reason You Work on Sundays)

If you’ve ever sat through a productivity seminar or scrolled through a 'thought leader's' LinkedIn feed, you’ve almost certainly heard of the Zeigarnik Effect. Discovered in 1927 by Lithuanian psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik, the theory goes that our brains are haunted by unfinished business. The classic story involves Vienna waiters who could remember massive, unpaid dinner orders perfectly, only for those memories to evaporate the second the bill was settled. For decades, we've been told that leaving tasks incomplete is a brilliant way to keep them fresh in our minds.

Except, it turns out, that’s mostly rubbish. A landmark meta-analysis by Romain Ghibellini and Beat Meier at the University of Bern analysed nearly a century of research on the topic. Their verdict? The classic Zeigarnik Effect—the idea that you have a superior memory for unfinished tasks—lacks universal validity and completely failed to show a reliable effect. In our modern world of Slack pings, WhatsApp notifications, and endless multitasking, our brains do not magically remember incomplete work. In fact, interruptions just ruin our memory.

But the researchers did find something else that is highly robust: the Ovsiankina Effect. Named after Maria Ovsiankina (a colleague of Zeigarnik), this effect describes our innate, subconscious urge to resume and complete interrupted tasks, even when there is absolutely no external reward or incentive to do so. An unfinished task creates a 'quasi-need'—a state of psychological tension and cognitive dissonance. We don't remember the half-written report any better, but we are absolutely desperate to finish it just to scratch the mental itch.
The Sunday Afternoon Trap

This explains a lot of weird workplace behaviour. Have you ever found yourself opening your laptop on a Sunday afternoon to finish a slide deck or reply to a non-urgent email, despite promising yourself you’d have a proper weekend? You aren't doing it because you're a hyper-dedicated corporate warrior. You’re doing it because of the Ovsiankina Effect. The cognitive dissonance of leaving that task 80% done is creating a physical weight in your brain. You aren't working to be productive; you're working for psychological relief.

You can also see this in sales and client management. If you send a prospect a blank 10-page onboarding questionnaire, they’ll ignore it. But if you pre-fill 8 pages with their public company data and leave only 2 pages blank, the Ovsiankina Effect kicks in. The 'incomplete' state of the document creates a psychological tension that compels them to fill in the rest and send it back.
How to Use It

items: The Monday Morning Hack (The Hemingway Trick): Instead of killing yourself to finish every single task on Friday afternoon, deliberately leave a structured, easy-to-finish task 90% complete. Write the first half of an email, or leave the final formatting of a model for Monday. When you log in on Monday morning, the Ovsiankina Effect will give you an immediate, effortless urge to dive in and finish it, bypassing the usual Monday morning dread.

The 'Incomplete' Pitch: When pitching to senior stakeholders, don't present a perfectly polished, finished product that leaves them with nothing to do. Leave a small, structured 'gap' or a clear next step for them to co-create or complete. Their brains will naturally want to close the loop, driving higher engagement.

Protect Your Focus: Recognise that every time you start a task and get interrupted, your brain creates a new 'quasi-need' loop. If you have five half-finished tasks open, you aren't just multitasking; you are carrying a massive cognitive load of psychological tension. Close the loops or don't start them in the first place.

content.text: "Don't rely on your brain to remember unfinished tasks (Zeigarnik is a myth); rely on its desperation to finish them (Ovsiankina is real)."

sources.title: Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects
sources.publisher: Springer Nature (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications)
sources.note: This landmark meta-analysis analysed nearly a century of research, debunking the Zeigarnik effect while validating the robustness of the Ovsiankina effect.

Electronic Arts went private in a historic $55bn LBO backed by Saudi Arabia's PIF and Silver Lake.
Mastercard spent up to $1.8bn on BVNK, betting heavily on stablecoins for cross-border B2B payments.
A critical Coldcard firmware bug drained $110m in Bitcoin, driving massive inflows into institutional spot ETFs.
